rows: The agent proposes changing a test so the build goes green

Block and keep the judging tests locked: SWE-bench judges a patch against tests split from the human pull request and applied at evaluation, outside the model's input; the source does not discuss an agent editing tests, so blocking is a harness rule built on that design (`jimenez-swe-bench`) • Block: the checks that judge the agent are trusted computing base and must sit beyond its reach; a human changes them, with a reason (`openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai`) • Block until the change has a recorded reason, a named person who agreed it and the reviewer's view: plan changes are raised with the commissioner and documented, and the assurer gives feedback on them. Locking the tests is a harness rule (`uk-aqua-book-2025`) • Block unless a spec change requires the new expectation; the source allows test updates when functionality changes and forbids creating expected outcomes from the code's own output (`uk-duck-book-qa-of-code`) • Ask which file changes: a feature-file edit changes the agreed behaviour and goes back to whoever agreed it, since the documentation holds that a scenario's intent stays the same when the implementation changes (`cucumber-bdd-gherkin`). Locking the scenario is a harness rule • Block: a unit test's failure should indicate a bug, and a test moved to match the implementation stops signalling a safe change (`microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook`) • Block the edit and return the failing test to a human: the report's foreword records AI silently deleting tests (`dora-ai-assisted-swdev-2025`). Locking the tests is a harness rule • Block and route the change to the test's owner as a recorded decision: by transfer, check criteria are defined and tracked, their records protected from alteration, and code owners approve others' changes (`nist-ssdf-1-1`) • Block and return it to a human with a reason: agents are kept from self-adjusting objectives beyond predefined parameters, and editing the test is the agent adjusting its own goal (transfer) (`owasp-agentic-threats-mitigations`) • Block: an agent that games a flawed metric produces misleading results, and a test moved to reach green is the metric gamed rather than the behaviour fixed (`owasp-agentic-top10-2026`, reward hacking applied to a coding agent as a transfer)
The tests were written by the same agent session after the code

Before they count, run each on the base commit and see it fail for the right reason, then pass with the change: every SWE-bench test was validated that way; the source did not measure agent-written tests (`jimenez-swe-bench`) • Treat as asserted until their strength is measured: agent suites written from a spec passed the correct build 88-96% of the time yet killed 38-56% of planted faults; same-session tests were not measured, so carrying this over is an inference (`egashira-testsuitebench-2026`) [D8] • Run them on the old code and require a test that failed there: test before fix, and validation is independent reproduction, not self-review (`openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai`) [D8] • Treat them as the build's own assurance and require the reviewer's further checks against cases the build didn't write: verification and validation are planned at design, and the assurer carries out further verification and validation (`uk-aqua-book-2025`) • Treat as asserted; require expected values traced to the intended behaviour; the source says the best practice is to write tests before logic and that test data must reflect how the code should work, not how it currently works (`uk-duck-book-qa-of-code`) • Treat as asserted: the documentation calls automating after the code reasonable test automation "but it's not BDD", and its method automates each agreed example before the code (`cucumber-bdd-gherkin`) • Treat as a description of current behaviour; check against the planned cases, since the playbook writes tests early and test-first (`microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook`)
A test checks the agent's output text rather than the system's state

Decide the outcome by applying the change and running the tests against the changed code: that is the source's resolution rule (`jimenez-swe-bench`) • Block until it asserts on the system: checks must measure target behaviour, not their own artefacts (`openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai`) • Require `Then` steps to assert on output observable to the user or an external system (`cucumber-bdd-gherkin`) • Require assertions on the logic: a test that only checks what the double returned would pass even if the logic were wrong (`microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook`) • Rewrite it to check the state the output claims: the source names incorrect state inference and an agent reporting a backup that never ran as failures that land when output is trusted and acted on (`owasp-llm-top10-2026`) • Check the system's state: deceptive behaviour keeps the appearance of compliance, and the guide's coding agent produced false test results (`owasp-agentic-threats-mitigations`)
The suite passes, but nobody knows whether it would catch a wrong implementation

Require each target test to have been seen failing on the old code: execution-based validation keeps a test only if it moves from fail to pass (`jimenez-swe-bench`) • Require a strength measure on the ledger: seed faults that each break one requirement, drop tests that fail on the correct build, and count what the suite kills (`egashira-testsuitebench-2026`) [D8] • Require a known-bad run before trusting the suite: a broken or mis-aimed verifier can confidently approve an incorrect result (`openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai`) • Run the tests against reference cases with known answers: complex work is ideally tested against independent reference cases, and black-box assurance should verify the automatic tests themselves (`uk-aqua-book-2025`) • Partial: require a run record showing each new scenario failing before the code, so it at least can fail (`cucumber-bdd-gherkin`); strength against wrong builds needs seeded faults (`egashira-testsuitebench-2026`) • Ask which inputs the tests state as intended behaviour and add negative cases: a suite at 100% coverage still missed a bug (`microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook`) • For an injection defense, require a red-team run by someone given the defense: a study the source cites found static attack success near zero beside adaptive success above 90% for most of 12 defenses (`owasp-llm-top10-2026`)
The suite takes minutes, so it runs rarely

Make it faster and run it on every change: if CI takes too long, CI becomes the bottleneck (`openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai`) • Require every test on every change in CI; the source says to run all tests against each change and that automated runs build trust by ensuring all unit tests pass before every merge (`uk-duck-book-qa-of-code`) • Make the unit suite run in seconds on every change and move slow tests to the PR gate; sleeps and disk reads are the usual cause (`microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook`) • Make the tests fast enough to run on every change: when AI speeds up development, control systems must speed up too, starting with faster feedback loops (`dora-ai-assisted-swdev-2025`) • Require the vulnerability tests in the automated pipeline on every change: automated analysis and testing run regularly or continuously for every supported release (`nist-ssdf-1-1`) • Run the security checks on every build: abuse-case tests check controls each build, and application-specific verifications can sit on the existing unit and integration test infrastructure for continual verification (`owasp-asvs-5-0`) • Automate the model's tests in the pipeline as regression tests; ongoing scanning and testing rely mainly on automation (`nist-sp-800-218a`)
A new test's failure on the base commit is an ImportError or AttributeError
Don't count it as fail-to-pass: the authors removed such failures as possible dependency-naming errors (`jimenez-swe-bench`)
The locked tests have no pass-to-pass set
Lock the existing tests over what the change touches as pass-to-pass: a run can pass every target test and still break prior behaviour (`jimenez-swe-bench`)
The agent's suite has far fewer tests than the spec has behaviours

Require at least one meaningful test per documented behaviour: suites smaller than the requirements scored lower, and Sol's were about five times smaller than the reference (`egashira-testsuitebench-2026`)
Each feature is tested once, with a single or default input
Require a test using the input combination that would expose a wrong build: omitted combinations were the commonest miss in the error analysis (`egashira-testsuitebench-2026`)
A test asserts only the shape of the output (length, non-empty, a keyword appears)
Require the assertion to pin the content the requirement fixes: a shape-only check passed a completion script for the wrong shell (`egashira-testsuitebench-2026`)
"Give the agent the running program and it will write better tests"
Keep the ask on test design: with the reference executable, Sol's validity rose from 94.4% to 98.4% and its mutation score stayed at about 38% (`egashira-testsuitebench-2026`)
"Turn up the reasoning effort" or "use the bigger model" for the tests
Expect marginal gains: cost and strength follow a log curve, Sol rose from 31.3% to 46.5% from low to xhigh effort, and the best agent reached 55.5% (`egashira-testsuitebench-2026`)
A check fires on the broken build but has not been run on the fixed build or on benign input
Run the counterfactual before accepting the check: a reported rerun found published checks firing on patched versions and benign input (`openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai`)
A test's expected values were produced by running the new code
Block; rebuild expectations from the specification on minimal hand-written data, since copied output assumes the function already works (`uk-duck-book-qa-of-code`)
A mocked test never asserts that the mock was called
Require the assertion; the source warns that a broken mock can let a real request run while tests still pass (`uk-duck-book-qa-of-code`)
A diff edits a feature file's expected outcome alongside the code
Split the edits and route the feature-file change to whoever agreed the scenario; behaviour need not change because the implementation does (`cucumber-bdd-gherkin`)
A `Then` step definition queries the database
Rewrite it to check observable output: the reference tells readers to "resist that temptation" (`cucumber-bdd-gherkin`)
Declarative scenarios read well, but nobody has read the step definitions behind the `Then` steps
Read them: in the declarative style the exact values live in the step definitions, so that is where the assertion is decided (`cucumber-bdd-gherkin`; the reading is the distillation's inference)
A test sleeps, reads an expected value from disk or calls a live third-party API
Block: each breaks the speed, isolation or reliability a unit test needs; wrap the dependency and replace the sleep with a reliable state signal (`microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook`)
The tests verify the exact sequence of calls the implementation makes

Flag: behavioural verification ties the test to the implementation, so the next refactor breaks it and invites an edit to the test; prefer state checks or fakes (`microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook`)
The plan leaves the agent to write the key tests for its own build

Write the key tests before the run, outside the agent: preliminary evidence finds autonomous agents leave key tests out; locking them first is the distillation's inference (`becker-metr-ai-developer-productivity-2025`)
An agent change adds code with no tests alongside it, or coverage is checked only as a whole-codebase percentage
Require coverage on the added lines: the authors suggest test coverage requirements that scale with lines added (`he-cursor-velocity-complexity-2025`)
Login or registration is tested only on success

Add abuse-case tests that run on every build: for the username, default usernames, enumeration, brute force, LDAP and SQL injection and XSS; for the password, common passwords, length, null bytes, a removed parameter and XSS (`owasp-asvs-5-0`)
The change retrains or fine-tunes a model, or adds a data source to its training, and the model's tests are not rerun
Block until the new data's integrity and provenance are checked and the model is retested: retest models when retrained or given new data sources (`nist-sp-800-218a`)
A model feature's test plan holds unit tests only
Require the test types the risk calls for (integration, penetration, red teaming, use case, adversarial), automated as regression tests (`nist-sp-800-218a`)
An LLM feature's injection tests cover only the user's input field
Extend them to plant instructions in retrieved content, tool output, files and memory: defenses that watch only the chat surface miss indirect injection (`owasp-llm-top10-2026`)
An agentic feature's defences have never been attacked, or it has no goal-override red-team test, memory-rollback test or replay test

Red-team it with simulated poisoned components and supply-chain attacks before release (`owasp-agentic-threats-mitigations`) • Require them before the build: red-team goal override and check that rollback works, adversarial unit tests, memory snapshots and rollback, and replay of recorded agent actions in an isolated clone (`owasp-agentic-top10-2026`)
An LLM feature's tests include no prompt outside its coverage, or every test expects an answer

Add out-of-coverage and no-document prompts that expect abstention, scored so a wrong answer costs more than an abstention: a suite where every test expects an answer is binary grading, under which abstaining never scores (`why-language-models-hallucinate-kalai`)
